in inﬂammatory responses and may affect cognition (Godos et al., 2020), possibly by decreasing reactive intermediates in the brain.
Several studies within the PKU population reveal micronutrient deﬁciencies in vitamins B2, Niacin (B3), B12, D, zinc, and sele-
nium, among others. Current data suggests that supplementation with micronutrients, both individually and within medical foods,
has improved the nutritional status in those living with PKU, however, supplementation from medical foods may be insufﬁcient
(Lammardo et al., 2013) and concentrations in the blood may remain low (Nazari et al., 2016). The mechanisms for utilization of
micronutrients in the PKU population and the bioavailability of the micronutrients added to medical foods are not sufﬁciently
researched (Nazari et al., 2016).
Individuals living with PKU may be at signiﬁcantly higher risk of deﬁciency of vitamins B2, Niacin (B3), B12 due to the lack of
vitamin B rich foods in the diet and other theorized mechanisms (Brantley et al., 2018). The risk of B vitamin deﬁciencies is greater
in those individuals with PKU not under medical supervision (Schoen et al., 2019). Vitamin B supplementation is warranted in the
PKU population when not obtaining adequate amounts of these vitamins from medical food (Kose and Arslan, 2019) or when
